slides.0.title: Meet Canadian Wine
slides.0.subtitle: From wild grapes and native vines to VQA and icewine: the history of Canadian wine
slides.1.title: Early days: from Vinland to commercial wineries
slides.1.highlights.0.title: The Vinland saga
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Norse sagas say that around AD 1001 Leif Ericsson found grapes and named the place Vinland; wild grapes did grow along the eastern seaboard (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Schiller in 1811
slides.1.highlights.1.content: In 1811 Johann Schiller, a retired German corporal, planted a small vineyard from wild vine cuttings on the Credit River west of Toronto and sold the wine to neighbours; calling him the father of the Canadian wine industry is called perhaps overstated (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Pelee Island in 1866
slides.1.highlights.2.content: In 1866 the first true commercial winemaking operation began on Pelee Island with 30 acres of Catawba; by 1890 Canada had 41 commercial wineries, 35 of them in Ontario (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
slides.1.content: Early Canadian wine relied on wild, native and cold-hardy vines.
slides.2.title: Prohibition and the modern starting point
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Winemaking survived Prohibition
slides.2.highlights.0.content: During Prohibition (1916–1927) making and selling wine stayed legal, and Canadians could buy sweet "ports" and "sherries" at 20% alcohol by volume; provincial liquor boards were set up afterwards to regulate alcohol (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: The start in BC
slides.2.highlights.1.content: In the 1860s the first BC vineyards were planted near Kelowna at Father Charles Pandosy's Oblate Mission; the first Okanagan winery came only in the 1930s (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Inniskillin in 1975
slides.2.highlights.2.content: In 1975 Donald Ziraldo and Karl Kaiser founded Inniskillin and were granted a winery licence by the LCBO; Winealign calls it the first since 1929 (often described as the first since Prohibition, so accounts differ). In the same period small family wineries in Ontario and BC began to challenge the large producers
slides.2.content: Modern Canadian wine begins with the small wineries of the 1970s.
slides.3.title: Transformation: VQA and icewine
slides.3.highlights.0.title: The birth of VQA
slides.3.highlights.0.content: VQA was created by Ontario wineries in 1988 as a voluntary industry programme, with Ziraldo as founding chair, and brought to BC in 1990. The Vintners Quality Alliance Act, 1999 was proclaimed on 29 June 2000 and the first VQA wine was approved on 10 July 2000 (Wine With Seth, Winealign)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: The BC vine-pull
slides.3.highlights.1.content: A vine-pull programme in 1988–1990 uprooted about 65% of BC's existing vineyards, which were replanted with vinifera (Wine With Seth); BC's Wines of Marked Quality Regulation came into force on 1 August 2005 and was replaced by a new version in 2018
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Icewine makes the name
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Inniskillin's Karl Kaiser harvested its first Vidal icewine in 1984 (Winealign); in 1991 Inniskillin's 1989 Vidal icewine won the Grand Prix d'Honneur at Vinexpo in France; The Canadian Encyclopedia calls Ontario the world's largest icewine producer
slides.3.content: Institutions around 1988 and the success of icewine shaped the modern image of Canadian wine.
